snippet.title: Will This Whisky Save Rajsthan's State Bird Godawan?
snippet.description:
Will This Whisky Save the Godawan? Aman Sharma
The Great Indian Bustard, once flying freely from Rajasthan to Tamil Nadu, is now one of the top 10 most endangered species in the world.
British hunting, habitat destruction, and deadly power lines wiped out almost the entire population — and today, only a few dozen Godawans remain.

In 2022, the liquor giant Diageo launched Godawan Whisky, promising that a portion of its sales would support conservation. The whisky won awards, gained popularity, and earned crores…
But the Godawan bird?
It continued disappearing.

Despite being Rajasthan’s state bird, despite government schemes, despite campaigns — the truth is harsh:
The whisky will survive. The bird may not.

This is the story of how a critically endangered species became a marketing symbol instead of being saved.

snippet.title: One Texas High School’s Efforts to Help Students Graduate (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
snippet.description:
An unforgettable look at the lives of four students who were in crisis and the teachers, counselors and principal who fought to get them to graduation. (Aired 2012)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

What does it take to ensure a student graduates? That question was at the center of FRONTLINE’s 2012 documentary “Dropout Nation.” At the time, hundreds of thousands of teenagers in the United States were quitting high school without diplomas. The massive dropout rates hindered individual career prospects and clouded the country’s future. 

Sharpstown High School in Houston, Texas, which had earned a reputation as a “dropout factory,” launched a high-stakes experiment to address this problem. FRONTLINE spent a semester immersed in Sharpstown High  exploring the challenges students faced trying to stay in school and the struggles educators encountered to keep them there.

 A troubling and inspiring journey, “Dropout Nation” investigated the causes, challenges and potential solutions of a national emergency.

“Dropout Nation” was written and produced by Frank Koughan. It was produced by Kevin Vargas. The co-producer was Lisa Kalikow. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

snippet.title: How This Man Selling Vada Paw Built a ₹500 Crore Fast Food Empire!
snippet.description:
How This Man Selling Vada Paw Built a ₹500 Crore Fast Food Empire! Aman Sharma
In 2001, Dheeraj Gupta noticed that Mumbai sold over 20 lakh vada pavs every day, yet most stalls lacked hygiene and consistency. With a ₹2 lakh loan from his father, he launched Jumbo King, offering hot, fresh, clean, and standardized vada pav — something India had never seen before.

The idea exploded. Jumbo King soon started selling 40,000 vada pavs every single day. But Dheeraj didn’t want to stay limited to Mumbai. He dreamed bigger. He introduced affordable burgers and began expanding across India.

Today, with 200+ outlets nationwide, Jumbo King is India’s third-largest burger chain, all built from the simplicity of one iconic street food: vada pav.

A ₹500 crore empire born from a humble snack — this is the incredible story of turning a local favourite into a national brand.

snippet.description:
FRONTLINE and ProPublica trace the Trump administration’s federal immigration sweeps in major cities across the country — and the violence, protests and arrests stemming from them. 

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

How did the operations by masked and heavily armed federal agents, sometimes backed by the U.S. military, unfold in major cities like Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis? And how did protesters and bystanders who are U.S. citizens get caught up in the crackdown? Those questions are at the center of this documentary collaboration from FRONTLINE and ProPublica. 

The Trump administration said its immigration crackdown was protecting U.S. citizens by targeting criminals and people who had entered the country illegally. “Caught in the Crackdown” traces how what began as immigration enforcement operations also became something different — with the government arresting hundreds of U.S. citizens who were protesting or observing the raids, and routinely portraying those citizens as domestic terrorists or extremists.

But despite the rhetoric, the reality behind those arrests has often been quite different, ProPublica and FRONTLINE found: “When we analyzed more than 300 of these arrests, we found that while there have been successful prosecutions, over and over, cases have been falling apart, contradicted by video evidence and witness testimony,” says correspondent A.C. Thompson.

Video footage and witness testimony also contradicted official accounts of the circumstances surrounding the deaths of two protesters in Minneapolis, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, at the hands of ICE agents. 

It also traces the role of one of the key players in the operations, Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who defended the aggressive tactics and arrests and called them “exemplary.” After Pretti’s killing, Bovino was moved out of his role and has since retired, with the Trump administration saying it “recognized that certain improvements could and should be made” to its immigration enforcement operations.

snippet.description:
How an Indian Student Became an MLA in Russia! Aman Sharma
Abhay Kumar Singh left Patna in 1991 to study medicine in Russia, struggling with harsh weather and an unknown language. After returning to India without much success, he went back to Russia, built businesses in pharmaceuticals and real estate, and slowly rose in influence. In 2015, he joined Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, and by 2017 he was elected deputy from Kursk. His close connection with people helped him win again in 2022 — turning a simple boy from Bihar into a powerful figure in Russian politics.

snippet.title: How a Poor Teacher Built the World’s Largest Clock Company! Aman Sharma
snippet.description:
How a ₹55 Salary Teacher Built the World’s Largest Clock Company! Aman Sharma
Odhavji Patel was a school teacher in Gujarat, earning just ₹55 per month—barely enough to feed his six children. But instead of accepting his fate, he took a bold risk.

In 1971, he borrowed ₹1 lakh and started Ajanta Clocks from a small room, selling affordable wall clocks. The problem? These clocks needed regular winding, which customers hated.

To solve this, Patel travelled to Japan, learned Quartz technology, and launched India’s first quartz clocks—accurate, low-maintenance, and affordable. The market exploded.

When factory work slowed because male workers were busy farming, his daughter-in-law stepped in, convincing hundreds of village women to join the factory. This decision transformed production and stability.

By the 1990s, Ajanta had become the world’s largest wall clock manufacturer, proving that innovation, persistence, and the right people can turn even a ₹55 salary into a global legacy.
